newsitem.title: USA: Bankruptcy wipes slate clean - but the stigma lingers.
newsitem.headline: Bankruptcy wipes slate clean - but the stigma lingers.

text.p: Bankruptcy may not sound like an appealing way to dig yourself out of a financial hole. But Americans are increasingly declaring bankruptcy as an easy way to wipe the slate clean.

"The surprising thing is you need not be bankrupt to file for bankruptcy. You get to walk away from debts you voluntarily incurred. It's extraordinary relief," said William Binzell, vice president for government relations at Mastercard International.
"You can still have a steady source of income. They don't look at your ability to repay from future income. You're eligible even if you have assets."
As a result, a record 1.1 million Americans -- or 1 percent of all U.S. households -- filed for bankruptcy in 1996, and the number is estimated to reach 1.4 million this year.
To be sure, most people choose bankruptcy as a last resort -- which is what lawmakers originally intended it to be.

"Bankruptcies are by and large caused by a complex series of legal and social factors," said David Sandor, director of public affairs at Visa. These include the sudden loss of a job, medical emergencies and divorce.
The easy availability of credit cards has also led many consumers to the brink, leaving card issuers to shoulder the debt burden -- and pass costs on to other consumers.

"If someone doesn't know there's an alternative or they buy into the advertising that says bankruptcy is an easy way out, all they need is filing fee," said Durant Abernethy, president of National Foundation for Consumer Credit.
However, Abernethy added: "We believe at least 20 percent or more people filing bankruptcy who want to pay their bills could (avoid it)."
The Foundation's Consumer Credit Counselling Service (800-388-2227) provides free guidance for people in financial trouble.

Seventy percent of all people who file for bankruptcy choose Chapter 7, which in most cases allows forgiveness of almost all debts. The filer may keep all or part of personal property, such as clothes and furniture, Social Security and public assistance payments, pension accounts and a minimum amount of equity in a car and/or a personal residence.

Chapter 13 provides for debt repayment under a schedule worked out with courts. But only 30 percent of those who file for personal bankruptcy take this route because it is a costly, time-consuming and often inflexible process.
While most debtors who file for bankruptcy may believe they have no other way to stay above water, creditors are finding a growing number of fraud cases.
"Many are using (bankruptcy) as a financial management tool instead of last resort," Sandor said.

In Florida, creditors suspect fraud in about 5 percent to 10 percent of Chapter 7 bankruptcies, said Scott Spradley, a lawyer in Orlando, Fla., who has represented credit card companies in bankruptcy court for about eight years.
It's been characterised as "stealing," he said. "Instead of going into bank and walking into an unlocked vault, they're using the credit card as the key to an unlocked vault."

One of the red flags is a sudden change in the spending pattern of credit card holders. For example, a usually conservative consumer may use up his credit limit and make large luxury purchases just before filing for bankruptcy.

Because of the escalating bankruptcy costs, credit card issuers and financial institutions formed the Bankruptcy Issues Council in January to advocate legal reforms that would make it harder to file for bankruptcy.

"People who have ability to repay a portion of debt should be required to pay that portion because ultimately, the debt is passed on to other consumers in terms of higher prices for goods and services and credit," said Mastercard's Binzell.
Even if you can wipe out your debts with a bankruptcy filing, your slate isn't exactly clean.
"It's hard to get credit again. It can affect your job prospects, buying a house or even renting a place," Abernethy said.
A Chapter 7 filing stays on your credit report for seven years, and you cannot file Chapter 7 again for another six years.

"If you haven't learned anything and live beyond your means, you face Chapter 13 and have to use your income to pay off your bills. You face a three- to five-year court supervised payment plan," Abernethy said.

To avoid credit problems -- and bankruptcy -- stop using credit if you think your debts are getting too big to handle. Let your creditors know if you're going to skip payment or be late. Creditors are surprisingly willing to negotiate lower interest rates or payments rather than see a debtor default.

Come up with a realistic debt repayment plan. Consider part-time jobs. However, be wary of consolidation loans, Abernethy advised. Many consumers have lowered their payments but gotten into even more debt, he said.
